paraphrase: The sages know two modes of rasāyana: entering a hut (kuṭīprāveśika) and 'wind-and-sun' (vātātapika, in ordinary life). For the first, a hut with three chambers is built in a safe town with provisions, away from disturbing sounds and women; at an auspicious time the person, head shaved, having made firm his resolve, memory and strength, faithful and collected, casting off the mental doṣas and cultivating friendliness to beings, worships the gods and brahmins and enters; purified by cleansing therapies and restored in strength, he then takes the rasāyana.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: Procedure, diet and preparations deliberately omitted (summary only).

paraphrase: Medicine is twofold: some gives vigour to the healthy, some cures the diseased. What gives vigour to the healthy is rasāyana or the aphrodisiac. From rasāyana one gains long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, excellence of lustre, complexion and voice, great strength of body and senses, success of speech, respect and radiance; rasāyana is the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other dhātus.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: That which gives offspring and immediate delight, by which a man goes like a stallion to women unobstructed, is dear to them, and whose semen remains fruitful even in age, and by which, with many children like a tree with many branches, he is honoured and gains continuity of lineage here and endlessness hereafter — that is vājīkaraṇa.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The juice of maṇḍūkaparṇī, the powder of liquorice with milk, the juice of guḍūcī with its root and flower, and the paste of śaṅkhapuṣpī give life, destroy disease, increase strength, fire, complexion and voice; these rasāyanas are intellect-promoting (medhya), śaṅkhapuṣpī above all.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Entering the hut is wholesome for the capable, healthy, wise and self-controlled who have leisure and means; for others the wind-and-sun mode; the former is the better but very hard to carry out. If diseases arise from a lapse in the rasāyana regimen, they are to be treated with their own remedies, setting the rasāyana aside.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Once the sages, living in villages on village food, became heavy, slow and unfit; recognizing the fault of village life they went to the Himalaya, where Indra welcomed them: 'village life is the root of the blameworthy; it is time to attend to your bodies and time for Āyurveda, which the Aśvins gave me as Prajāpati gave it to them.' He transferred to them the nectar of Āyurveda and showed them the divine herbs of the Himalaya, now in their potency.
speaker: Indra

paraphrase: Know as enjoying constant rasāyana the man who is truthful, free of anger, abstaining from liquor and sex, non-violent, not over-exerting, calm, pleasant of speech, given to recitation and purity, steady, ever generous and austere, devoted to worshipping gods, cows, brahmins, teachers and elders, ever kind and compassionate, balanced in waking and sleep, taking milk and ghee, knowing place, time and measure, skilled in yukti, free of ego, of approved conduct, not mixing with the corrupt, with senses turned toward the inner self, serving the elders, the believers and the self-controlled, devoted to the dharma treatises. One endowed with these qualities who uses rasāyana obtains all its benefits.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: A person who has not removed his bodily and mental doṣas, at least grossly, never attains the benefits of rasāyana; the formulations for long life and against old age and disease succeed only for those pure in mind and body and self-restrained. This teaching is not to be told to the depraved, to those not twice-born who are not ill, or to those without the wish to serve.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The physician of good character, wise, disciplined, twice-born and master of the science is to be honoured by living beings like a guru, for he is the teacher of life (prāṇācārya). At the completion of study a physician has a second birth; he gains the name 'vaidya' not by his former birth; at the completion of learning the brāhma or ārṣa mind surely enters him through knowledge, so the physician is called twice-born.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Āyurveda was revealed by great sages devoted to dharma, desiring the imperishable state, for dharma, artha and kāma. One who practises healing neither for wealth nor for pleasure but out of compassion for beings surpasses all; those who make healing a commodity for livelihood abandon a heap of gold to pursue a heap of dust. There is no gift greater than the gift of life; one who treats thinking compassion for beings the highest dharma attains his aims and the greatest happiness.

paraphrase: In cauterization too the strength (authority) belongs to the physicians of Dhanvantari's school.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The physician examines complexion, voice, smell, taste, touch, the senses, mind, devotion, purity, character, conduct, memory, form, constitution and its deviations, strength, lustre, intelligence, cheer and the rest; normal states follow birth, family, place, time, age and the individual; deviations are either caused by marks fixed in the body by destiny, or by observable causes, or resemble causes — the last, appearing without cause, physicians take as signs of the measure of life and of death approaching.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Dreams are known to be sevenfold: of what was seen, heard, experienced, longed for, imagined, presaging (bhāvika), and born of the doṣas.

paraphrase: Exogenous insanity arises from the gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, teachers, elders and siddhas. Some hold past unwholesome karma to be its cause; Ātreya says its cause is prajñāparādha alone: through it a man disregards the gods and the venerable and does unwholesome acts, and they strike one already struck by himself. Its remedies are mantra, herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, observances, vows, expiation, fasting, benedictions, prostration and pilgrimage. Neither gods nor gandharvas, piśācas nor rākṣasas afflict a man not already afflicted by himself; for a disease born of prajñāparādha, one's own karma, the wise should blame neither gods nor ancestors nor demons but know himself as the agent of his happiness and suffering, and take the path of the good without fear.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: Summary only for the branch on possession: no rites or procedures recorded.

paraphrase: Diseases of old age and death, arising from the transformation of time, are natural and without remedy. The former-body karma called daiva is also, in time, a cause of diseases; there is no great karma whose fruit is not reaped; karma-born diseases that resist treatment subside with the exhaustion of that karma.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Neither senses nor objects are the causes of pleasure and pain; the cause is the fourfold contact (balanced, excessive, deficient, wrong); without self, sense, mind, intellect, object or act there is no pleasure or pain. Contact is twofold, bodily and mental. Craving (tṛṣṇā), consisting of desire and aversion, arises from pleasure and pain and is again their cause; it grasps the seats of feeling; without grasping there is no contact, and without contact no feeling. The seat of feelings is the mind and the body with the senses, excluding hair, nails, food, wastes and fluids.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: In yoga and in liberation all feelings cease; in liberation the cessation is complete, and yoga leads to liberation. Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of self, senses, mind and objects; when, through non-initiation, the mind is steady and established in the self, both cease and mastery (vaśitva) arises in the embodied one — this the sages who know yoga call yoga.

paraphrase: Entering (another body), knowing others' minds, acting on things at will, (divine) sight and hearing, memory, radiance, and invisibility at will — this is declared the eightfold power (aiśvarya) of yogins; all of it arises from concentration of the purified mind.

paraphrase: Liberation is the separation from all conjunctions, through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma; it is called non-return (apunarbhava).

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Serving the good and avoiding the wicked, vows and fasts and the various restraints, upholding the dharma treatises, understanding, delight in solitude, aversion to objects, resolve for liberation, supreme steadiness, not starting actions and exhausting those done, going forth (naiṣkramya), freedom from ego, seeing danger in conjunction, concentration of mind and intellect, examination of the truth of things — all this comes from the presence of the recollection of truth (tattvasmṛti); memory arises from serving the good down to steadiness, and remembering the nature of things one is freed from suffering.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Memory arises from eight causes: grasping the sign and form, similarity, contrast, attention (sattvānubandha), repetition, the yoga of knowledge, and hearing again; remembering what was seen, heard and experienced is called memory.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: This is the one path of liberation shown by the liberated, the strength of the recollection of truth, by which those who went have not returned; the yogins have called it the path of yoga, and the liberated Sāṃkhyas, who count the dharmas, the path of liberation.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: All that has a cause is suffering, not one's own, and impermanent; it is not made by the self, yet ownership arises there. As long as the true understanding 'this is not I, this is not mine' does not arise (one is bound); knowing it, the knower passes beyond all. In that final renunciation all feelings with their roots, with perception, knowledge and understanding, cease entirely. Thereafter the self, become brahman (brahmabhūta), is not perceived — freed from all states, it has no mark; this is the knowledge of the knowers of brahman, which the ignorant cannot know.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The five elements with consciousness as the sixth are the person (made of six dhātus); the consciousness-dhātu alone is also called the person; and by division of dhātus the person is of twenty-four: mind, the ten senses, the five objects and the eightfold prakṛti.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The mark of the mind is the presence or absence of knowledge: when self, sense and object are in contact, knowledge does not arise without the mind's presence. Atomicity and oneness are the two qualities of mind. Its objects are what is to be thought, considered, reasoned, meditated and resolved; its acts are directing the senses, restraining itself, reasoning and consideration; then buddhi, which is determinate, operates, and by it one decides to speak or act.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Agniveśa asked: into how many dhātus is the person divided? Why is the person a cause, what is its origin? Is it ignorant or a knower, eternal or not? What is prakṛti, what are the modifications, what the mark of the person? The knowers of the self call it inactive, independent, self-controlled, all-pervading, witness — then how does it act, why is it born in undesired wombs, why does it not know all feelings? Which comes first, the field or its knower? Which feeling — past, present or future — does the physician treat? Where do all feelings cease entirely, and by what marks is the one who knows all, has renounced all and is at peace, known?
speaker: Agniveśa

paraphrase: The aggregate of twenty-four is called the person; this conjunction, when joined with rajas and tamas, is endless; when they are removed by the increase of sattva it ceases. Here are established action and its fruit, knowledge, delusion, pleasure and pain, life and death, ownership; one who truly knows this knows dissolution and arising, the succession, treatment, and whatever is to be known.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: If the person did not exist there would be no light and darkness, truth and falsehood, Vedas, good and bad deeds, agent or knower, support, pleasure or pain, going and coming, speech, knowledge, sciences, birth and death, bondage and liberation; therefore the knowers of causes call the person the cause. Whoever says the body is made by the instruments without an agent, as a pot without a potter or a house without a builder, is outside reason and scripture; the person is known as cause by all the means of knowledge.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Some hold that the aggregate of momentary things, without a lord, called sattva, is the agent and enjoyer, not a person; for them what is done by some would be reaped by others that are new — they who teach no self. The instruments are seen to be other, and the agent the same; the agent joined with instruments is the cause of all actions. Things perish faster than a blink; what is broken does not return and what is done does not pass to another; hence the knowers of truth hold the eternal person to be the cause in action and enjoyment.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: The opponents described are not named; the view (momentary aggregate, no self) matches the Buddhists as reported by an opponent — the text reports it.

paraphrase: Ego-sense, fruit, action, passage to another body and memory exist only when there is a cause (the self) apart from the body. The supreme self, being beginningless, has no origin; the person called the aggregate (rāśi) is born of delusion, desire, aversion and action. The self is the knower; its knowledge operates through connection with instruments and does not operate when they are impure or absent — as one looking into a dirty mirror or muddy water sees nothing, so when the mind is afflicted.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The beginningless person is eternal; what is caused is the opposite. The unmanifest (avyakta) — the self, the knower of the field, eternal, all-pervading, imperishable — is other than the manifest; the eightfold prakṛti is the unmanifest, buddhi, ego-sense and the five elements; the sixteen modifications are the ten senses, mind and the five objects. All this except the unmanifest is the field; the sages know the unmanifest as the knower of this field.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: From the unmanifest arises buddhi, from buddhi the sense 'I', from ego-sense space and the rest in order; then the person, complete in all limbs, is said to be born; at dissolution he is separated from these. Possessed by rajas and tamas he goes from unmanifest to manifest and manifest to unmanifest, turning like a wheel; for those attached to the pairs of opposites and devoted to ego there is arising and dissolution, not for those who are otherwise.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Breathing in and out, blinking, life, movement of mind, passing from sense to sense, impelling and holding, travel to other places in dream, perceiving death, knowing with the left eye what is seen by the right, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, steadiness, intellect, memory and ego-sense are the marks of the supreme self; since these are found in the living and not in the dead, when it has gone the body is an empty house, unconscious, 'gone to the five' (dead).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The mind is unconscious though active; the self, the conscious one, is called the agent because it is conscious; the embodied self, though all-pervading, feels only in its own tactile sense and does not know feelings located elsewhere; it is all-pervading and great, and by concentration of the mind the self sees even what is concealed. Know it as bound constantly to the mind, which follows the body's acts, present in all wombs though abiding in one.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The self has no beginning, nor has the succession of fields; since both are beginningless, one cannot ask which came first. The knower is called the witness, since all things of all beings have the self as witness. The single self is never known by marks; it has no distinction; the distinction by feeling belongs to the conjoined person (saṃyoga-puruṣa).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The physician treats feelings of all three times: a returning headache or fever is a past feeling come again, and medicine given at its time allays the past; seeing prodromes and acting beforehand destroys the future one, as one builds a dike against waters that once ruined the crop; and the continuing chain of suffering is stopped and happiness set going by attending to its causes — like produce like: the balanced do not become unbalanced nor the unbalanced balanced of themselves.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Thus the physician removes feelings of the three times; but the final (naiṣṭhikī) cure is that which is without upadhā. Upadhā (craving-grasping) is the supreme cause that gives suffering and the seats of suffering; renunciation of all upadhās removes all suffering. As the silkworm takes up the threads that bring its death, so the ignorant, ever afflicted, takes up craving from objects; the knower, knowing objects to be like fire, turns away from them, and through not starting and not joining, suffering does not reach him.

paraphrase: The causes of suffering are the lapse of intellect (dhī), resolve (dhṛti) and memory (smṛti), the arrival of time and karma, and contact with unsuitable objects. Seeing the eternal and non-eternal, wholesome and unwholesome wrongly is the lapse of intellect; the mind prone to objects cannot be restrained from the unwholesome when resolve lapses; memory of truth lapses in one covered by rajas and delusion. The inauspicious act done by one whose intellect, resolve and memory have lapsed is prajñāparādha, the provoker of all doṣas — forcing or suppressing urges, rash acts, excess in sex, untimely action, loss of modesty and good conduct, insulting the venerable, knowingly using the harmful, friendship with the wicked, envy, pride, fear, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication; the wrong knowing and wrong acting of the intellect is prajñāparādha, for it is the mind's domain.

original.edition: Carakasaṃhitā, DCS e-text (sources_raw/dcs); verse = the e-text's counter (vulgate numbering)

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The self is never without the subtle supersensible elements, nor without karma, mind, intellect and the faults of ego; the mind bound by rajas and tamas is, with strong karma, the cause of going and acting. The causes of all diseases are prajñāparādha, wrong objects and time, and their allaying is by knowledge, objects and time rightly joined; righteous acts bring joy, others grief. The stream of body and mind has no beginning; its cessation is made by supreme steadiness, memory and understanding. One who eats and lives wholesomely, acts after examination, is unattached to objects, generous, equanimous, truthful, forgiving and serves the authoritative becomes free of disease; diseases do not fall on one whose thought, speech and act lead to happiness, whose mind is disciplined and intellect clear, who has knowledge, austerity and devotion to yoga.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: There is a mind arising of itself that joins the jīva to the body; when it is about to leave, character changes, the senses suffer, strength declines and one gives up life. This mind, which grasps the senses' objects, is threefold — pure, rājasa and tāmasa; with whichever the mind is most endowed, with that it is joined in the next birth, and when it is joined with the pure one remembers even past births; such a man is called 'one who remembers births'.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: When a man of unimpaired semen and a woman of unimpaired womb unite at the proper time, the jīva descends into the union of semen and blood within the womb through its conjunction with mind, and the embryo forms; it grows through wholesome nourishment and care. The embryo arises from the union of these factors: it is born of the mother, of the father, of the self, of suitability (sātmya) and of nourishment (rasa), and there is also the mind that arises of itself (aupapāduka sattva).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Bharadvāja: no. Mother, father, self, suitability and food do not produce the embryo, nor does a mind come from another world: if parents produced it, all who wanted sons would have them; the self cannot produce itself whether born or unborn, and if it could it would choose only desirable wombs; it is not from suitability or food, since the reverse is seen; and if a mind came from another world it would remember something of its former body.
speaker: Bharadvāja

paraphrase: The embryo is self-born: the inner self of the embryo, called the jīva, is eternal, free of disease, ageless, deathless, imperishable, not to be cut or pierced, of all forms and all acts, unmanifest, beginningless, endless; entering the womb and uniting with semen and blood it produces itself as the embryo. Its birth is only its passage from one state to another. Neither embryo, mother, father nor self has full freedom: they act partly by their own will, partly by karma. Mastery, action, birth and liberation are in the self's power; no other is the agent of pleasure and pain.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The three bodily doṣas corrupt the body, the two mental doṣas — rajas and tamas — the mind. Mind is threefold: pure (free of fault, having the auspicious part), rājasa (faulty, having the part of anger) and tāmasa (faulty, having the part of delusion); each has innumerable varieties, since body follows mind and mind body. As examples: the pure mind is sevenfold, after Brahmā, the ṛṣis, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera and the Gandharvas (the Brāhma being purest); the rājasa sixfold, after the asuras, rākṣasas, piśācas, serpents, pretas and birds; the tāmasa threefold, after beasts, fish and plants.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The root of engagement is delusion, desire, aversion and karma; from them spring ego-sense, attachment, doubt, false identification, possessiveness, wrong conviction, non-discrimination and wrong means, which overgrow a man like trees over a sapling; ego-sense is 'I am endowed with birth, beauty, wealth, learning, family'; attachment is any act of mind, speech and body not directed to liberation; doubt is 'do karma, its fruit, liberation, the person, the afterlife exist or not?'; sprinkling, fasting, the fire-sacrifice, three daily baths, entering water and fire and the like are called wrong means. So bound, he does not pass beyond engagement, the root of evil.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Disengagement (nivṛtti) is release (apavarga): that is the supreme, the tranquil, the imperishable; that is brahman; that is liberation.

original.edition: Carakasaṃhitā, DCS e-text (sources_raw/dcs); verse = the e-text's counter (vulgate numbering)

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The ways for those seeking liberation: seeing the faults of the world, one approaches a teacher, follows his instruction, tends the fire, follows the dharma treatises and understands them; serves the good and avoids the wicked; keeps away from company; speaks truth good for all beings, gentle and timely; regards all beings as oneself; does not remember, think of, desire or speak with women; renounces all possessions — a loincloth, an ochre robe, a needle, a water-pot, a staff, a bowl, one meal of whatever comes, a bed of fallen leaves, a band for meditation, a homeless forest dwelling; avoids sleep and sloth; restrains attachment to objects; acts with mindfulness in sleeping, standing, walking, looking, eating and every movement; bears honour and insult, hunger and cold; is unshaken by grief, pride, greed, passion, fear and anger; regards ego-sense as an affliction; contemplates the likeness of world and person; never tires of yoga; directs the senses into the mind, the mind into the self; repeatedly counts the body's parts by the dhātus; accepts that all that has a cause is suffering, not one's own and impermanent; sees evil in all engagement and happiness in total renunciation. This is the path to release; otherwise one is bound.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: Includes the renunciant's requisites and contemplation of the body; no restricted practice.

paraphrase: By these means of purification the impure mind (sattva) becomes pure, like a mirror polished with oil, cloth and brush; unclouded by planets, clouds, dust, smoke or mist, it shines like the sun's disc; enclosed in the self it burns steady like a lamp in a windless place. That pure understanding by which one breaks the great darkness of delusion, knows the nature of all things and becomes desireless, accomplishes yoga, becomes a Sāṃkhya, does not take up ego, grasps nothing and renounces all, and goes to the eternal, ageless, tranquil, imperishable brahman — it is called knowledge (vidyā), success, understanding, intelligence and wisdom.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: For one who sees himself spread in the world and the world in himself, who sees the higher and the lower, peace rooted in knowledge does not perish. For the brahman-become who sees all things in all states always, there is no conjunction; being pure, no mark of the self is perceived, for there are no instruments; freed from all instruments he is called liberated. Sinless, passionless, tranquil, supreme, imperishable, unchanging, deathless, brahman, nirvāṇa — these are names of peace.

paraphrase: Ātreya: 'this person is the measure of the world'. As many embodied kinds of things as there are in the world, so many in the person. The six dhātus — earth, water, fire, air, space and the unmanifest brahman — together are called person and world. Earth is the person's form, water its moisture, fire its heat, air its breath, space its cavities, brahman its inner self; as brahman's glory in the world is Prajāpati, so the inner self's in the person is mind; Indra corresponds to ego-sense, the sun to taking-in, Rudra to anger, Soma to serenity, the Vasus to happiness, the Aśvins to lustre, the Maruts to enthusiasm, the Viśvedevas to the senses and their objects, darkness to delusion, light to knowledge; creation is conception, the Kṛta age childhood, Tretā youth, Dvāpara old age, Kali disease, and the end of the ages death.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: For one who sees the whole world in himself and himself in the whole world, true understanding arises; seeing the world in himself he knows that he alone is the agent of his pleasure and pain; knowing 'I am the whole world', knowledge is first aroused for liberation. The world here means the aggregate of the six dhātus; its cause, arising, growth, affliction and dissolution are the world's nature. The knowledge that engagement (pravṛtti) is suffering and disengagement (nivṛtti) happiness is the truth.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: On which part of the embryo forms first there are many opposed views among the sages who composed treatises: the head, being the seat of the senses (Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja); the heart, seat of consciousness (Kāṅkāyana); the navel, where nourishment enters (Bhadrakāpya); the rectum, seat of wind (Bhadraśaunaka); hands and feet, the person's instruments (Baḍiśa); the senses, seats of intellect (Janaka of Videha); it cannot be thought, being beyond perception (Mārīci Kaśyapa); all limbs form at once (Dhanvantari). Ātreya: Dhanvantari's view is right, since all things are mutually bound; seeing things as they are is good.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: On timely and untimely death: some say whoever dies dies at his time, for time has no gaps — that is not right; others say the time one dies is his fixed time of death — that too misreads the matter. Timeliness and untimeliness are seen directly, as in the world rain and cold and flowers come in season and out of season; so both exist, death in time and out of time. If there were no untimely death all life-spans would be fixed, knowledge of the wholesome would be useless and the means of knowledge that reveal what prolongs and shortens life would be invalid; the sages regard 'there is no untimely death' as mere words.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: In this age the measure of life is a hundred years; its causes are excellence of constitution, qualities and self, and the use of what is suitable.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Ten are the seats of life (prāṇāyatana): the head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: A different list of ten stands at Sū 29.3 (temples, the three vital points, throat, blood, semen, ojas, anus).

paraphrase: The redactor expands what is said briefly and condenses what is too long, and makes an old tantra new; this best of tantras, redacted by the very wise Caraka, is found lacking a third; to complete it unbroken, Dṛḍhabala, born in the city of Pañcanada, having propitiated Śaṅkara, gleaned from many tantras and filled in seventeen chapters on medicines, and the Siddhi and Kalpa sections.
speaker: Dṛḍhabala

paraphrase: The tantra is adorned with thirty-six devices of exposition (tantrayukti) — topic, connection, purpose of reason, meaning of a word, partial statement, enumeration, definition, ellipsis, purpose, instruction, citing a reason, extension, implication, decision, recapitulation, the unqualified and the qualified, exception, the contrary, prima facie view, rule, assent, explanation, doubt, backward and forward reference, technical term, the inferable, aggregation, example, etymology, combination, option, rebuttal, restatement, possibility. As the sun opens a lotus pond and a lamp lights a house, they awaken and illumine a tantra; without them a physician, though studying the texts, does not reach their meaning; a science badly grasped harms the ignorant like a weapon, well grasped it protects.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: The DCS e-text reads ṣaḍviṃśatā ('26'), but the list names thirty-six; standard editions read ṣaṭtriṃśatā.

paraphrase: He in whose heart this saṃhitā of twelve thousand dwells knows meaning and reasoning and is skilled in treatment. What is here is found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere.

A medicine not properly known is like poison, a weapon, fire or a thunderbolt; properly known it is like nectar. Even a sharp poison becomes the best medicine by right application, and a medicine wrongly applied becomes a sharp poison.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The sages entered meditation and saw with the eye of meditation Śakra as their refuge; Bharadvāja volunteered and was sent; he went to Indra's abode and asked, on the sages' behalf, for the means of allaying the diseases that frighten all creatures; Indra taught him Āyurveda in few words, seeing his great understanding.

paraphrase: By it Bharadvāja gained immeasurable, happy life and taught it to the sages without holding anything back; the sages, seeing with the eye of knowledge general (sāmānya) and particular (viśeṣa), qualities, substances, action and inherence, followed the method of the tantra and gained supreme well-being and long life.
speaker: the narrator

paraphrase: Bharadvāja, of fierce austerity, seeking long life, went to Indra, knowing him to be the refuge of the gods. Prajāpati first received Āyurveda entire as Brahmā taught it; from him the Aśvins; from the Aśvins Śakra (Indra); and the seer Bharadvāja approached Śakra.

paraphrase: That is called Āyurveda in which are told the wholesome and the unwholesome, the happy and the unhappy life, what is wholesome and unwholesome for life, its measure, and life itself.

paraphrase: The substances are space and the other four elements, the self, mind, time and the directions; a substance with senses is conscious, without senses unconscious. The qualities are the sense objects, the twenty beginning with heavy, buddhi, and those from 'para' to effort; action is movement; inherence is the inseparable relation of earth and the rest with their qualities; the substance is the inherent cause in which action and qualities reside.

paraphrase: Thus cause and effect have been told; equilibrium of the dhātus is the effect sought here, and the action that brings it about is declared the purpose of this tantra.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Wrong, deficient and excessive contact of time, intellect and sense objects is the threefold cause of diseases, which have two seats; the body and what is called mind are the seats of diseases, as also of well-being, whose cause is balanced contact.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The supreme self is changeless; together with mind, the qualities of the elements and the senses it is the cause of consciousness; it is eternal, the seer who sees actions.

paraphrase: Vāyu, pitta and kapha are the collection of bodily doṣas; rajas and tamas are declared the mental ones. The former are allayed by medicines resting on the divine and on reasoned application; the mental by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (samādhi).

paraphrase: Vāta is dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear and rough, and is allayed by substances of opposite qualities; pitta is slightly unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, flowing and pungent; the qualities of kapha — heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, sweet, stable and slimy — are allayed by their opposites.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: When diseases arose among embodied beings as obstacles to austerity, fasting, study, continence, vows and life, the great sages of meritorious deeds, putting compassion for beings first, assembled on the auspicious flank of the Himalaya — Aṅgiras, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, Gautama, Sāṃkhya, Pulastya, Nārada, Asita, Agastya and many others — treasuries of the knowledge of brahman, of self-control and restraint.
speaker: the narrator

paraphrase: Disorders held curable turn back through medicines of opposite qualities applied according to place, dose and time; no means of cure is taught for the incurable.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Taste (rasa) is the object of the tongue; its material basis is water and earth, with space, air and fire as causes of its formation and differences. Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter and astringent — this is the collection of six tastes. Sweet, sour and salt overcome vāyu; astringent, sweet and bitter pitta; astringent, pungent and bitter kapha; and in reverse they provoke.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Ātreya: medicine with its four pillars and sixteen qualities, rightly applied, is sufficient for health. Maitreya: no — some patients with every support recover and others with the same die, and some without any support recover and others die; so medicine is no different from no medicine. Ātreya: that is wrong thinking; for diseases curable by medicine, medicine is not causeless; those who recover without full treatment would recover sooner with it, as a fallen man helped up rises faster; not all diseases are curable, and the curable are not cured without means. We treat the ill by what is not ill, fill deficient dhātus and reduce excess, and restore the normal state.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: All is twofold, existent and non-existent; its examination is fourfold: authoritative testimony (āptopadeśa), perception, inference and yukti. The authorities (āpta) are those freed from rajas and tamas by the strength of austerity and knowledge, whose knowledge of the three times is pure and unobstructed; their word is true. Perception is the clear cognition arising from contact of self, sense, mind and object; inference, based on perception, is of three kinds and three times (fire from smoke, intercourse from pregnancy, fruit from seed). Yukti is the understanding that sees things produced by the conjunction of many causes, valid for the three times, by which the three aims are achieved. There is no other examination; by it rebirth exists.

original.text: dvividhameva khalu sarvaṃ saccāsacca tasya caturvidhā parīkṣā āptopadeśaḥ pratyakṣam anumānaṃ yuktiśceti

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The authoritative scripture is the Veda and any other teaching not contrary to it, composed by examiners, approved by the learned and set forth for the good of the world; from it we learn that giving, austerity, sacrifice, truth, non-violence and continence bring prosperity and the highest good. Liberation (non-return) is not taught at the doors of dharma to those whose mental doṣas are not overcome; rebirth has been seen and taught by earlier sages of divine sight, free of fear, passion, hatred, greed, delusion and pride.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Here a man of unimpaired mind, intellect, manliness and valour who looks to his good in this and the other world should pursue three desires (eṣaṇā): for life, for wealth and for the other world. The desire for life comes first, for abandoning life is abandoning everything; it is kept up by the regimen of the healthy and vigilance in treating disease. Next comes wealth, for nothing is more wretched than a long life without means: farming, cattle-keeping, trade, royal service and other blameless occupations.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Rebirth is also perceived: children differ from their parents; those of the same origin differ in complexion, voice, form, mind, intellect and fortune; birth high and low, servitude and lordship, happiness, length of life, the untaught crying, sucking and laughing of infants, marks, different fruits of equal acts, intelligence in some work and dullness in another, memory of former births, like and dislike at first sight. From these one infers the unavoidable, imperishable karma of a former body called daiva, of which this is the fruit, and that another birth will follow; yukti: birth from the union of the six dhātus, fruit only of what was done, no sprout without seed.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Rebirth being established by the four means, one should attend to the doors of dharma: service of the teacher, study, vows, marriage, begetting children, supporting dependents, honouring guests, giving, absence of covetousness, austerity, absence of envy, unsullied acts of body, speech and mind, examination of body, senses, mind, objects, intellect and self, and concentration of mind; so one gains fame here and heaven hereafter.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The three supports (upastambha) are food, sleep and continence (brahmacarya); upheld by these three rightly applied, the body continues endowed with strength, complexion and growth for its full span, provided one does not indulge in what is unwholesome.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Strength (bala) is threefold: innate (natural to body and mind), temporal (from season and age) and acquired (from diet and activity).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The three bases of disease are excessive, deficient and wrong use of objects, of action and of time. Wrong action of body, speech and mind — suppressing or forcing urges, lying, harsh speech, and fear, grief, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy and wrong view — is to be known as prajñāparādha (failure of discernment). Time is also called transformation (pariṇāma). So unwholesome contact of senses and objects, prajñāparādha and pariṇāma are the three causes of disorders; balanced, they are causes of health.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Diseases are threefold: endogenous (from the bodily doṣas), exogenous (from poison, wind, fire, blows) and mental (from not getting the desired and getting the undesired). A wise man even when afflicted by mental disease should, examining with his understanding, avoid the unwholesome and pursue the wholesome in dharma, artha and kāma, and serve those who know them; the medicine for the mind is attention to the three aims, service of the wise, and knowledge of self, place, family, time and strength.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Physicians are of three kinds: pretenders who get the name from a physician's kit, books and glances; the 'reputed' who borrow the name of the famous; and those endowed with the qualities of a physician, accomplished in application, knowledge and understanding, givers of happiness and life — in these alone physicianship resides.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Therapy is threefold: resting on the divine (daiva-vyapāśraya) — mantra, herbs worn, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, gifts, oblations, observances, expiation, fasting, benedictions, prostration, pilgrimage and the like; resting on reasoned application (yukti-vyapāśraya) — the planned use of diet and medicines; and conquest of the mind (sattvāvajaya) — restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects.

original.text: trividhamauṣadhamiti daivavyapāśrayaṃ yuktivyapāśrayaṃ sattvāvajayaśca
original.edition: Carakasaṃhitā, DCS e-text (sources_raw/dcs); verse = the e-text's counter (vulgate numbering)
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: For bodily doṣas there is internal cleansing, external cleansing and surgical measures. A disease is at first small and afterward grows; rooted, it robs the fool of strength and life; the fool heeds it only when in pain and then begs his family to bring a physician at any cost — but who can save one already wasted? Therefore one wishing his own happiness should counter diseases beforehand, or while they are young.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Third is the desire for the other world. Here there is doubt whether we shall exist after departing hence. Some, holding to perception alone, take up denial (nāstikya) since rebirth is imperceptible; others accept rebirth on the strength of scripture alone; and scriptures differ. Some hold that mother and father are the cause of birth; others nature (svabhāva), creation by another (paranirmāṇa) or chance (yadṛcchā). Hence the doubt: is there rebirth or not?
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The wise should give up the notion of denial and doubt, for what is perceptible is little and what is imperceptible is much, known through scripture, inference and yukti; even the senses by which we perceive are themselves imperceptible. Existing things are not perceived because of excessive nearness or distance, obstruction, weakness of the sense, inattention of mind, mixture with similar things, being overpowered, or extreme subtlety; so to say 'only the perceptible exists' is unexamined.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Those scriptures (that make the parents the cause) are not valid, being against reason: if the self of mother or father passed into the child, it would pass whole or in part — whole, and the parent would die; in part, but the subtle self has no parts; and mind and intellect are the same. Of the six dhātus the specific nature is natural, but their union and separation are caused by karma; creation by another does not apply to the beginningless conscious dhātu — unless the 'other' is the supreme self. For the chance-theorist and the denier there is no examination, examiner, agent, gods, sages, siddhas, karma or fruit; the grip of denial is the sin beyond all sins. The wise should see all as it is by the lamp of the good.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Ātreya: you have all spoken rightly, except for the one-sidedness of each. Vāta, pitta and śleṣman in their normal state endow a man with unimpaired senses, strength, complexion, happiness and long life, as dharma, artha and kāma rightly practised bring him the great good here and hereafter; disturbed they bring the reverse, as the three seasons disturbed bring ruin to the world at its time of destruction.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Vāyorvida: vāyu, unprovoked, is the upholder of the body's structure and machinery; it is fivefold as prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna; impeller of all movements, controller and guide of the mind, employer of the senses, arranger of the dhātus, source of speech, cause of joy and enthusiasm, kindler of fire, expeller of wastes, maker of the embryo's form, and the support of continuing life. Provoked it afflicts body and mind. In the world it upholds the earth, kindles fire, drives sun, moon and stars, makes clouds and rain, divides the seasons; provoked it shatters mountains and ends the ages. Vāyu is the lord: source and imperishable, maker of being and non-being, Death, Yama, Prajāpati, Aditi, Viśvakarman, all-pervading, Viṣṇu.
speaker: Vāyorvida

paraphrase: In loss of ojas one is fearful, weak, anxious, with afflicted senses, poor lustre, dejected, dry and emaciated. Ojas, reckoned in the body as pure, slightly reddish-yellow blood residing in the heart, is that by whose destruction a man is destroyed; it is the first thing produced in the body of the embodied, ghee-coloured, sweet in taste and smelling of parched rice.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: When the mind is tired and the senses, tired, withdraw from their objects, a man sleeps. Happiness and misery, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness, virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, life and death depend on sleep. Sleep indulged at the wrong time or in excess takes away happiness and life like another night of doom; the same sleep rightly taken gives happiness and life, as true understanding comes to the yogin with accomplishment.

paraphrase: Sleep is born of tamas, of kapha, of fatigue of mind and body, is adventitious, follows disease, or arises from the nature of night. The knowers call sleep from the nature of night the nurse of beings (bhūtadhātrī); sleep born of tamas they call the root of sin; the rest they assign to diseases.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: As the sages disputed, Punarvasu said: do not speak thus; truth is hard to reach by taking sides. Those who argue thesis and counter-thesis as though settled never reach the end of the matter, like an ox at an oil-press going round. Give up this clash of arguments and reflect on the inner reality (adhyātma); knowledge of the knowable does not arise until the mass of darkness is shaken off. The very factors whose excellence produces the person produce, when impaired, his various diseases.

paraphrase: Asked what makes the person and diseases grow, Ātreya said: the use of wholesome food alone makes the person grow, and unwholesome food is the cause of disease. Wholesome is the food that keeps the balanced dhātus in their normal state and brings the unbalanced into balance; the opposite is unwholesome.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: In an assembly of sages King Vāmaka of Kāśī asked: are the person and his diseases born of the same source or not? Pārīkṣi Maudgalya: both are born of the self, for the self gathers karma and reaps its fruits. Śaraloman: no — the self would not yoke itself to suffering; the mind pervaded by rajas and tamas is the cause. Vāryovida: not the mind alone; beings and diseases arise from rasa (water). Hiraṇyākṣa: the self is not born of rasa; person and disease arise from the six dhātus, as the first Sāṃkhyas taught. Kauśika: without mother and father how could the six dhātus make a person? — they are the cause. Bhadrakāpya: the blind are not born of the blind; the creature and his diseases are born of karma. Bharadvāja: the agent precedes the act; nature (svabhāva) is the cause. Kāṅkāyana: from nature neither effort nor success would follow; the creator Prajāpati of unlimited will is the cause. Bhikṣu Ātreya: Prajāpati, ever wishing his creatures' good, would not yoke them to misery like a wicked man; time is the cause.
speaker: the assembled sages

paraphrase: Every substance is made of the five elements; the earthy is heavy, rough, hard, stable and gives bulk; the watery liquid, unctuous, cold and moistening; the fiery hot, sharp, light and burning; the airy light, cold, dry and drying; the spatial soft, light and porous. By this teaching there is nothing in the world that is not a medicine, when used with the right reasoning and for the right purpose.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: In the Caitraratha forest the sages discussed taste and diet. Bhadrakāpya: there is one taste, not other than water. Śākunteya: two, the eliminating and the pacifying. Pūrṇākṣa Maudgalya: three. Hiraṇyākṣa: four (sweet-wholesome, sweet-unwholesome, unsweet-wholesome, unsweet-unwholesome). Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja: five, earthy, watery, fiery, airy, spatial. Vāyorvida: six — heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry. Nimi of Videha: seven, adding alkali. Baḍiśa: eight, adding the unmanifest. Kāṅkāyana: innumerable. Ātreya: there are six tastes — sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent; their source is water; alkali is a substance, not a taste; the unmanifest is a state of taste; the innumerability belongs to their substrates, not to the tastes.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Substances hostile to the body's dhātus come into conflict with them — some by opposed qualities, some by combination, preparation, place, time or dose, some by nature. One should not eat fish with milk: both are sweet and very channel-clogging, but of opposed potency (cold and hot), so they vitiate the blood and obstruct the channels; many further incompatible combinations are named, some fatal. Whatever food provokes the doṣas without expelling them from the body is unwholesome.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya
notes: Individual combinations not reproduced beyond the first example.

paraphrase: Bhadrakāpya: all fish may be eaten with milk except the cilicima, which causes blood disorders and death. Ātreya: no — no fish at all should be eaten with milk, the cilicima especially, since it is very channel-clogging and rouses the poison of āma.
speaker: Bhadrakāpya and Ātreya

paraphrase: Ten are the seats where the vital breaths abide: the two temples, the three vital points (head, heart, bladder), the throat, blood, semen, ojas and the anus. Physicians are of two kinds: those who come to save lives and destroy disease, and those who come to disease and destroy lives — pretenders in a physician's garb who roam the streets for work, boast of themselves, run down the attending physician and ingratiate themselves with the patient's friends; the wise patient should avoid them as messengers of death.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Of things that prolong life the best is non-violence to living beings; of things that increase strength, vigour; of things that nourish, knowledge; of things that delight, mastery of the senses; of things that gladden, the realization of truth; of paths, continence (brahmacarya) — so think the knowers of Āyurveda.

paraphrase: If asked which of the four Vedas the knowers of Āyurveda follow, the physician should declare his devotion to the Atharvaveda, for the Veda of the Atharvans teaches healing by gifts, benedictions, offerings, auspicious rites, oblations, observances, expiations, fasting and mantras, and healing is taught for the good of life.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Life (āyus) is the continuance of consciousness; it is called Āyurveda because it makes known life by its own marks — happy and unhappy, wholesome and unwholesome — and its measure, and the substances, qualities and actions that promote or harm it. Happy life belongs to one free of bodily and mental disease, youthful, capable, rich in knowledge and enjoyments; wholesome life to one who desires the good of beings, does not take what is another's, is truthful, calm, examines before acting, is vigilant, pursues the three aims without conflict, honours the worthy, is devoted to knowledge and tranquillity, serves elders, controls passion, anger, envy, pride and haste, is ever generous, devoted to austerity, knowledge and peace, knows the inner self, and looks to this world and the next.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Its purpose is to protect the health of the healthy and to allay the disorder of the diseased.

paraphrase: This Āyurveda is declared eternal, because it is beginningless, because its characteristics are established by nature, and because the nature of things is eternal: there was never a time when the continuum of life or of understanding did not exist; the knower of life is eternal, and happiness and suffering with their causes are beginningless. No origin of Āyurveda from non-existence is found, except in the sense of its being understood or taught; it is with regard to these two that some speak of its origin.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Āyurveda has eight limbs: internal medicine, treatment of the head (śālākya), surgery, toxicology, the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), children's medicine, rejuvenation and virilization. It is to be studied by brahmins, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas — by brahmins for compassion to beings, by kṣatriyas for protection, by vaiśyas for livelihood, and by all for dharma, artha and kāma. The physician's supreme dharma is to cure those devoted to the inner self and to dharma, and his own kin and teachers, and to meditate on and teach the spiritual knowledge (adhyātma) Āyurveda contains; his artha is the livelihood and protection it brings; his kāma the honour and the health of those he loves.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The heart is called 'mahat' and 'artha': in it are established the six limbs, consciousness, the senses and their five objects, the self with its qualities, mind and its objects; it is the seat of the supreme (para) ojas and the gathering place of consciousness; from it spread the ten great vessels carrying ojas, by which all embodied beings live. To protect it and the ojas, avoid especially the causes of mental suffering, and diligently pursue what is good for the heart and ojas and clears the channels — above all calm and knowledge.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: This tantra has eight sections — Śloka (Sūtra), Nidāna, Vimāna, Śārīra, Indriya, Cikitsita, Kalpa and Siddhi — with thirty chapters in the Ślokasthāna, eight each in Nidāna, Vimāna and Śārīra, twelve in Indriya, thirty in Cikitsā, and twelve each in Kalpa and Siddhi.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: As the lord of a city is attentive to his city and the charioteer to his chariot, so should the wise man be attentive to the duties toward his own body. One should pursue those means of livelihood that do not conflict with dharma, and peace and study; thus one attains happiness.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: One should eat in measure; the measure of food depends on the strength of the digestive fire: that amount which is digested in due time without disturbing one's normal state is the right measure; food eaten in measure unfailingly brings strength, complexion, happiness and long life.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: As a pot, a leather and an axle become firm and resistant through oiling, so by oil-massage the body becomes firm, the skin good, vāta's afflictions are calmed and it bears strain and exercise; since touch is chiefly vāyu's and touch rests in the skin, massage is supremely good for the skin and should be practised regularly; one who massages daily is little touched by injury and is strong, pleasant to see and ages little.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The year has six parts by season; the sun's northern course is the 'taking' (ādāna) period of three seasons from winter's end to summer, and the southern course the 'releasing' (visarga) period from the rains to early winter. In the taking period sun and wind dry the world and increase the dry tastes, and men weaken; in the releasing period the moon is unobstructed and the unctuous tastes and men's strength increase. Strength is weak at the beginning and end, middling in between.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: But these urges one seeking good here and hereafter should restrain: the urges to rash, blameworthy acts of mind, speech and body; greed, grief, fear, anger and pride; shamelessness, envy, excessive passion and covetousness; harsh, slanderous, false and untimely speech; and bodily acts that harm others — sex with another's wife, theft, violence. One whose acts of mind, speech and body are free of sin is 'meritorious' and enjoys and accumulates dharma, artha and kāma happily.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The wise should not suppress the arisen urges of urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, and breathing after exertion; diseases arise from suppressing them.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Bodily exertion that brings steadiness and strength is called exercise; it should be done in measure. It gives lightness, capacity for work, steadiness, endurance of hardship, reduction of doṣas and kindling of the fire; excess brings fatigue, exhaustion, wasting, thirst, bleeding disorders and other ills. One who indulges in exercise, laughter, talk, travel, sex or waking beyond measure perishes like a lion dragging an elephant.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The wise should withdraw from an accustomed unwholesome thing gradually and take up the wholesome gradually; doṣas reduced gradually and good qualities built up gradually do not return and remain unshaken.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Some men are from conception of balanced pitta, vāta and kapha; some are vāta-, pitta- or kapha-dominant; the first are free of disease, the others always prone to it; the bodily constitution is named after the doṣa that lies predominant in them. For them a regimen of opposite qualities is wholesome; for the balanced, the balanced use of all tastes.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Diseases from spirits, poison, wind, fire and injury come from a fault of discernment (prajñāparādha); envy, grief, fear, anger, pride, hatred and the like are mental disorders all born of prajñāparādha. Abandoning prajñāparādha, calming the senses, memory, knowledge of place, time and self, and following good conduct — this is the way to prevent adventitious disease; heeding authoritative instruction is the cause both of preventing and of curing disorders.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Men of sinful conduct, speech and mind, slanderers, lovers of quarrel, mockers, greedy, envious of others' growth, deceitful and pitiless are to be avoided; the elders in understanding, learning, age, character, steadiness, memory and concentration, calm, keepers of vows and speakers of the good path, are to be served.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Therefore everyone who wishes his own good should always, with mindfulness (smṛti), follow good conduct (sadvṛtta); following it one achieves two things at once, health and mastery of the senses. Then good conduct is taught in full: honour gods, cows, brahmins, teachers, elders, siddhas and ācāryas; tend the fire; wear auspicious herbs; bathe twice; keep the orifices and feet clean; be well dressed, cheerful and fragrant; speak first and pleasantly; help those in distress; offer oblations and gifts.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: One should not speak falsehood, take another's property, desire another's wife or wealth, delight in enmity or do evil; not speak of others' faults or pry into their secrets; not sit with the unrighteous, the insane or the degraded; not climb dangerous heights or bathe in violent water; not eat or study at the wrong time and place; not have intercourse at forbidden times and places; not despise women nor confide too far in them; not recite at inauspicious times; not associate with the greedy or foolish, nor take to drink, dice or courtesans; neither trust all nor suspect all.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: One should not let the time for action pass, nor act without examination, nor be ruled by the senses, nor let the fickle mind wander, nor overburden the intellect and senses; one should not follow anger and exultation, dwell in grief, be puffed up in success or dejected in failure; one should constantly remember (one's own) nature, be established in knowledge of cause and effect, not relax thinking 'it is done', not give up vigour, and not brood over reproach.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: One should be devoted to continence (brahmacarya), knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity and calm.

notes: The list maitrī, kāruṇya, harṣa (joy), upekṣā parallels the four immeasurables of the Yoga Sūtra and the Buddhists; noted as a cross-link only.

paraphrase: One who rightly follows the regimen of the healthy as taught lives a hundred years free of disease, fills the world of men with fame, is esteemed by the good, attains dharma and artha, becomes a friend of beings and, doing merit, goes to the worlds of the virtuous; therefore this conduct is to be followed by all at all times.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Beyond the senses is the mind, called sattva or cetas; its activity depends on the presence of its objects and of the self, and it is the cause of the senses' activity. Though in one person it seems many because of its varying objects and its conjunction with sattva, rajas and tamas, it is one — it does not operate on many objects at once; the mind is named after the quality that constantly accompanies it. The senses can grasp their objects only when led by mind.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Learning, reasoning, understanding, memory, devotion and practice — nothing curable escapes the one who has these six; learning, intelligence, practical insight, practice, success and support — each alone suffices for the name vaidya, but one who has them all truly deserves the name and gives happiness to beings.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Friendliness, compassion toward the afflicted, delight in those who can be cured, and equanimity toward beings who are going to their end — this is the fourfold conduct of a physician.

paraphrase: Physician, substances (medicines), attendant and patient are the four pillars (pāda) — the cause, when endowed with their qualities, of the allaying of disorder. Disorder is imbalance of the dhātus, their balance is the normal state (prakṛti); health is called happiness and disorder suffering. The activity of these four for the balance of the dhātus is called treatment (cikitsā).

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The physician's four qualities: clear grasp of the teaching, wide practical experience, skill and purity; the medicine's: abundance, suitability, many forms of preparation, potency; the attendant's: knowledge of nursing, skill, devotion to the patient, purity; the patient's: memory, obedience, fearlessness and ability to describe the illness. Of these sixteen-qualitied four, the physician — knower, instructor and applier — is chief, as the potter is to clay, stick and wheel.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: There are eight special factors of the rule of diet: the nature of the food (its natural qualities), its preparation (which imparts new qualities), combination, quantity, place, time, the rules of eating, and the eater himself, on whom habitual suitability depends.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The root of the vitiation of air and the rest is adharma, or the evil deeds of the past; the source of both is prajñāparādha. When rulers of lands and cities abandon dharma and rule unrighteously, their people increase that adharma; dharma is hidden, the gods forsake them, the seasons are disturbed, rain fails, the herbs lose their nature and disease follows. War and curses (from teachers and sages disregarded) likewise have adharma as their cause.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Before adharma there was no arising of the inauspicious. In the first age men were of immeasurable life, of great strength, truthful, free of fear, passion, grief and disease. As the Kṛta age declined, over-eating brought heaviness, then fatigue, idleness, hoarding, possessiveness and greed; in the Tretā greed brought malice, falsehood, lust, anger and fear; a quarter of dharma vanished, the qualities of earth and crops declined, and fever and other diseases arose; so life-span diminishes. In each age dharma declines by a quarter; one year of life is lost for every hundred years.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Asked whether all life-spans are fixed, Ātreya said: life depends on yukti; its strength and weakness rest on daiva and puruṣakāra. Daiva is one's own deed of a former body; puruṣakāra is what is done here. Each is of three strengths; strong daiva and strong effort give long happy fixed life; a weak daiva is overcome by effort and weak effort by strong daiva. Some karma ripens at a fixed time; some is not fixed and is roused by conditions; so one-sided views are wrong. If all life were fixed, no one seeking life would use mantras, medicines and rites, avoid wild animals, precipices or poison, and the sages' teaching on rejuvenation would be pointless.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: At Kāmpilya in Pañcāla, walking by the Gaṅgā with his pupils in the last month of summer, Ātreya told Agniveśa: the stars, planets, moon, sun, winds, fire and directions are seen to be abnormal; soon the earth will not give herbs their proper taste, potency and effect, and disease will follow; gather the medicines now, before the devastation.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: As an axle with all good qualities, carefully driven, comes to its end in time by the exhaustion of its own measure, so life in a strong constitution rightly cared for ends by the exhaustion of its measure — that is death in time; as the same axle breaks midway through overload, bad roads or bad driving, so life ends midway through exertion beyond strength, eating against the fire, irregular eating, excessive sex, bad company, suppression or forcing of urges, poisons, injury and neglect of food and remedies — that is untimely death.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Epidemics strike people of differing constitution, diet and strength at once through what they share — air, water, land and season — each harder to avoid than the last. Those whose death is not fixed survive by purifying therapies, rejuvenatives taken in due form, truth, compassion for beings, giving, offerings, worship of the gods, good conduct, calm, self-protection, dwelling in healthy lands, continence and the company of the continent, discussion of dharma with self-controlled sages, and constant company of the righteous.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Knowledge of disease is threefold: authoritative testimony, perception and inference. The authorities are those who know without speculation, free of attachment and aversion; the word of the drunk, insane, foolish, passionate or corrupt is not authority. Perception is what one grasps by the senses and mind; inference is reasoning that depends on yukti.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Excessive flow, obstruction, knotting of the vessels, or flow in a wrong path — these are the signs of vitiated channels.

paraphrase: As many as are the kinds of embodied things in the person, so many are its channels (srotas); no thing in the person arises or wastes without them; they carry the dhātus undergoing transformation. Some hold the person is only an aggregate of channels — not so. The channels are of prāṇa, water, food, rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, urine, faeces and sweat; the doṣas move through all of them; for the supersensible mind and the rest the whole conscious body is the channel and seat. Channel, vessel, duct, nāḍī, path, passage and space are names for them.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: Sattva is called the mind; it governs the body through its connection with the self. It is of three grades: superior, middling and inferior. Those of superior mind, even with small bodies, are not distressed by great pains; the middling sustain themselves by seeing others or are sustained by others; the inferior can be sustained neither by themselves nor by others and, even with large bodies, cannot bear small pains.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: There is no easy crossing to the far shore of Āyurveda; so one should apply oneself to it constantly and without heedlessness; and one should learn good conduct and freedom from envy even from others, for to the wise the whole world is a teacher, to the unwise an enemy; a word that brings wealth, fame, life and welfare should be heard and followed even from an enemy.

speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: A physician should converse with physicians, for discussion brings zeal for knowledge, confidence, eloquence and fame, removes doubts and brings to hearing what one had not heard; what a pleased teacher reveals step by step as secret, two disputants eager to win bring out together. Discussion is friendly (with a patient, knowledgeable, unpretentious partner — ask and answer with confidence, do not fear defeat or exult in victory, do not cling one-sidedly) or hostile (examine the opponent, the audience and one's own strength first). The wise do not delight in quarrels in an assembly of the good; an angry man will do or say anything.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: To know the course of debate among physicians these terms are to be learnt: debate (vāda), substance, quality, action, general, particular, inherence, proposition, establishment, counter-establishment, reason, example, application, conclusion, rejoinder, tenet, word, perception, inference, tradition, analogy, doubt, purpose, the inconclusive, desire to know, determination, presumption, probability, questionable and unquestionable, question and counter-question, faults and merits of speech, quibble, pseudo-reason, the untimely, censure, defence, abandoning the proposition, admission, shifting the reason and the topic, and the point of defeat. Vāda is disputation with another based on the science; it is jalpa (each side establishing its thesis, e.g. 'rebirth exists' against 'it does not') or vitaṇḍā (only finding fault with the other side).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The intelligent man who wishes to become a physician should first examine the treatise: choose one that is esteemed by the great and wise, rich in meaning, suited to the three kinds of students, free of repetition, of sage origin, well arranged, clear and illustrated. Then he should examine the teacher: of clear learning, seen in practice, skilled, dexterous, pure, with a trained hand, equipped, of sound senses, knowing constitution and procedure, of unpretentious learning, free of pride, envy and anger, patient, affectionate to pupils, a teacher able to make others understand. Approaching him, the student should serve him attentively like fire, a god, a king, a father and a master.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The means of mastery are study, teaching and discussion with those learned in the science. The method of study: rising early, after purification, bowing to gods, sages, cows, brahmins, teachers, elders, siddhas and ācāryas, sitting at ease in a clean level place, one should recite the aphorisms again and again with the mind attending to the words, understanding their meaning, to remove one's own faults and assess others'; so at noon, afternoon and night without fail.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The teacher should first examine the student: calm, noble in nature, not mean in action, of sound features and speech, steady, free of pride, intelligent, endowed with reasoning and memory, magnanimous, of a physician's family or conduct, devoted to truth, of sound senses, modest, not given to vices, fond of study, wholly devoted to understanding and practice, not greedy or lazy, wishing the good of all beings, obedient and attached to the teacher.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The ten things to be examined before action: the cause (the physician), the instrument (the medicine), the source of the effect (imbalance of the dhātus), the effect (their balance), the fruit of the effect (happiness), its continuation (life), the place (land and patient), the time (the year and the patient's state), the undertaking (the start of treatment) and the means (the excellence of physician and the rest).
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: At an auspicious time the teacher has the student, shaven, fasted, bathed and in ochre, bring fuel, fire, ghee and other requisites; he kindles the fire on a prepared altar, offers into it with benedictory mantras to Brahmā, Agni, Dhanvantari, Prajāpati, the Aśvins, Indra and the sages who composed the sūtras; the student circumambulates the fire. Then before fire, brahmins and physicians the teacher instructs him: be a celibate student, bearded, truthful, not eating meat, pure, free of envy, bearing no weapon; do what I say except what is hateful to the king, fatal, very unrighteous or harmful; live devoted to me like a son, servant and suppliant; seek the welfare of all living beings, cows and brahmins first; strive day and night with your whole self to relieve the sick; do not betray patients even for your life; do not in thought approach others' wives or covet others' goods. The student answers 'so be it'; one who so acts is to be taught, otherwise not.
speaker: Punarvasu Ātreya

paraphrase: The patient should be examined by constitution, morbid state, excellence of tissues (sāra), compactness, measure, suitability (sātmya), mind (sattva), capacity for food, capacity for exercise, and age — to know the measure of strength; for a strong medicine given without examination to a weak patient can kill him, and a weak one given to a strong patient with a strong disease is useless.

paraphrase: Constitution arises from the state of semen and ovum, the season and womb, the mother's diet and conduct, and the elements; the doṣa predominating there marks the embryo, so some are kapha-, some pitta-, some vāta-natured, some mixed, some balanced. The kapha-natured, from kapha's unctuous, smooth, soft, sweet, firm, dense, slow, stable, heavy, cold, slimy and clear qualities, are strong, wealthy, learned, vigorous, calm and long-lived; the pitta-natured are of middling strength, life and knowledge; the vāta-natured have little strength, life, wealth and memory; those balanced in all qualities are best.
